full_judgment:
The accused petitioner came to know about the case and the judgment and order of conviction passed against him only on 29.4.91 when he was arrested and thereafter produced before the Special Tribunal on 30.4.91 and sent to custody on the same date. After obtaining the certified copy the petitioner was confirmed about the judgment and order of conviction and thereafter filed the appeal which was reported as time barred though it is not so if time for filing the appeal is computed from the date of knowledge of the petitioner. Mr. AFM Shahid, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State, drawing our attention to the provision of section 30 of the Special Powers Act argued that section 29, sub-section (2) clauses (a) and (b) of the Limitation Act has no manner of application for condoning the delay in filing an appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act and as such the appeal cannot be heard on merit. The learned Deputy Attorney-General in support of his contention has relied on the case of Elahi Bux Vs. The State reported in 39 DLR 164 wherein on consideration of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act as a whole it was held that where a Special Law provides for limitation different from the first schedule of the Limitation Act the provision of sections 4, 9, 18 and 22 of the Limitation Act will apply for determination of the point of limitation unless those are excluded by special Law and the .remaining provision including section 5 of the Limitation Act will not apply unless it is made applicable by the Special enactment. In the light of the above discussion on interpretation of the section 29(2) of the Limitation Act dissenting from the Single Bench view taken in the case of Mustafizur Rahman Vs. State reported in 1985 BLD 335, the Division Bench of this Court expressed the view that section 5 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application for condonation of delay in filing an appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. 

 4. Being conscious about the restriction imposed for admission of an appeal arising out of a case under the Special Powers Act on condonation of delay invoking the aid of section 5 of the Limitation Act, Mr. Marfat Ali, the learned advocate, took a different stand in the matter asserting that the appeal is well within time and it requires admission for hearing on merit. The learned Advocate does not dispute that time for filing an appeal is 30 days from the date of judgment and order of the Special Tribunal under section 30 of the Act but contends that this method of calculation will not be applicable in respect of a case in which trial is held in absentia and in respect of a person who has no opportunity to appear and face trial. In the present case, the learned Advocate submits that the accused petitioner was absolutely in dark about the criminal proceeding against him and also about the judgment and order of the Tribunal on the date of its delivery till his arrest as no such order of the court was published in the official Gazette directing the accused to appear before the Tribunal in compliance of the provision of section 27(6) of the Special Powers Act and for that matter the judgment and order of conviction passed against the petitioner is a nullity. It is argued that the judgment and order of conviction being coram non judice the period of limitation will run not from the date-of judgment and order but from the date of knowledge of the order of conviction. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied on the case of Lal Mia Vs. the State reported in 42 DLR 15. In the said Single Bench decision it is held that the time for filing an appeal is to be counted from the date of knowledge of conviction. The above view is taken in an appeal arising out of a case under section 457 of the Penal Code in respect of which no special law of limitation has been prescribed. In the case of the above nature where limitation has not been specifically prescribed and trial is held in absentia the pronouncements by the superior courts, particularly by the Supreme Court, is laid down as a rule that nobody can be made to suffer any harm to his rights including those relating to property, person and reputation without giving him opportunity to show cause. 

 "It can be safely assumed that the proceedings without giving opportunity of hearing are coram non judice and the order passed as a result thereof is a nullity. And if the party affected by such an order had no knowledge of the same, the plea of limitation that it starts from the date of the order cannot be pressed against such an affected party. That party would be clearly entitled to challenge the order within the prescribed time counting the period from his knowledge." 

 5. The above principle is applicable in the cases where no specific bar is imposed in the statute. It may be left with the discretion of the court to decide as to whether the aggrieved party has been prevented by sufficient just and reasonable cause in not filing the appeal in time. But what will be the starting point of limitation in a case where the petitioner has been convicted under the special law is the question posed before us. Mr. Marfat Ali submits that the period of limitation will run from the date of knowledge in a case where the judgment and order has been passed in the absence of the aggrieved party.  6. The above principle has been laid down in a case of civil nature and where there is provision for filing appeal by the person aggrieved by the order. The case before us is quite different from the case cited.
